body:
Why a digital identifier needs privacy safeguards

A digital identifier is useful because different services can refer to a particular individual. However, repeated use of the same identifier may create risks if organisations unnecessarily collect it, retain copies or combine records from unrelated activities. Such practices can expose personal information and make it easier to link information across services.

Privacy safeguards aim to limit unnecessary disclosure while allowing legitimate verification. UIDAI provides options that distinguish identification from disclosure of the complete Aadhaar number.

Virtual ID and masked Aadhaar

FeatureMeaningImportant distinction
Virtual ID (VID)A temporary, revocable 16-digit random number mapped to an Aadhaar number.Can be used instead of the Aadhaar number for supported authentication or e-KYC processes.
Masked AadhaarAn Aadhaar representation that hides the first 8 digits and shows only the final 4.Reduces disclosure of the complete 12-digit number.
Biometric lockA UIDAI security facility that restricts biometric authentication while the lock applies.Helps prevent unwanted biometric use; other permitted authentication modes may remain available.

VID cannot be used to derive the underlying Aadhaar number. It is therefore different from merely covering part of the printed Aadhaar number. Masking reduces exposure when displaying or sharing a document, but it does not itself constitute a new authentication method.

Online authentication and offline verification

Online Aadhaar authentication involves an authentication request processed by UIDAI. It depends on the authorized authentication process and supporting connectivity.

Offline verification allows identity-related information to be checked without making an online Aadhaar authentication request to CIDR for that transaction. For example, UIDAI's secure, digitally signed Aadhaar QR code can be checked using an appropriate verification application. The signature helps establish whether the relevant data originated from UIDAI and whether it has been altered. Aadhaar Paperless Offline e-KYC is another mechanism through which the holder can share digitally signed identity information for permitted verification.

Offline verification does not mean that an organisation may collect or retain unlimited personal information. Applicable consent, purpose and data-handling requirements still matter.

When Aadhaar authentication fails

Failure can arise from an incorrect entry, unavailable network, sensor problem, damaged fingerprint, illness, injury or an age-related difficulty. Such a failure does not automatically establish that the individual is ineligible for a service.

The amended Section 8(2) of the Aadhaar Act requires a requesting entity to provide prescribed alternate and viable means of identification when authentication fails because of illness, injury, age-related infirmity or technical or other reasons. For voluntary Aadhaar use, Section 4(6) requires requesting entities to inform holders of alternate and viable means of identification and not deny services for refusing or being unable to undergo authentication; Section 4(7) provides for mandatory authentication when required by a law made by Parliament.

Alternatives are particularly important for people without a registered mobile number, persons unable to use a particular biometric method, and residents of areas with unreliable connectivity. The particular alternative must follow the rules applicable to the service.

Three separate safeguards: VID reduces disclosure of the underlying Aadhaar number; masked Aadhaar conceals most of the displayed number; an alternative verification method helps prevent exclusion when a particular authentication route cannot be completed.

Prelims focus

  • VID is a temporary and revocable 16-digit alternative identifier for supported Aadhaar services.
  • Masked Aadhaar displays the last 4 digits and hides the first 8.
  • A digitally signed secure QR code can support offline Aadhaar verification.
  • Offline verification is different from an online CIDR authentication request.
  • Section 8(2) provides for alternate identification following specified authentication failures.
  • Trap: A failed biometric authentication attempt does not by itself prove that a genuine beneficiary is ineligible.

[Sources: UIDAI, 'My Aadhaar,' Virtual ID, masked Aadhaar and biometric lock services; UIDAI, 'Authentication,' Virtual ID and biometric locking sections; UIDAI, 'Aadhaar Paperless Offline e-KYC,' privacy and security sections; Aadhaar Act, 2016, amended sections 4(6), 4(7), 8 and 8A; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Online authentication sends a request through UIDAI and CIDR; offline verification checks signed information without a new CIDR authentication request.
pictures.caption: Online authentication and offline verification use different methods of checking Aadhaar-related information.

title: Aadhaar Privacy Safeguards, Offline Verification and Alternatives to Failed Authentication

body:
Why a person may need multiple digital accounts

A citizen may use separate websites for certificates, educational services, banking and other activities. If each website maintains a separate account, the person may need to remember different usernames and passwords and repeatedly complete similar registration steps.

Single Sign-On (SSO) allows a user to authenticate through a common sign-in arrangement and then access multiple participating applications, subject to their access permissions. A single login experience can reduce repeated authentication and improve convenience.

SSO describes the user experience and associated authentication arrangement. It does not, by itself, reveal whether all services store their records in one database or whether separate organisations independently manage their systems.

What is identity federation?

Federated identity is an arrangement in which an identity provider supplies authentication information, and sometimes permitted identity attributes, to another participating service that relies on that information.

The main participants are:

  • User: The person requesting access to a service.
  • Identity provider (IdP): The trusted service that authenticates the user and provides an appropriate confirmation.
  • Relying party: The application or organisation that accepts the identity provider's confirmation and decides which service functions the user may access.

For example, a citizen could seek access to an educational portal through a common identity provider. The portal redirects the sign-in process to the trusted identity provider. After successful authentication, the provider sends an accepted confirmation to the portal. The portal then decides whether the authenticated user can view a particular record or submit a particular application.

Federation does not remove authorization

A successful identity-provider response tells a relying application something about the user's authenticated identity. It does not automatically grant access to every record held by that application. The application still needs to apply its own authorization and eligibility rules.

Likewise, a federated login does not necessarily permit unlimited sharing of personal data. The information exchanged should be limited to what is required and permitted. Trust arrangements, secure communication, user consent where applicable and clear institutional responsibility are important.

Comparing separate accounts, SSO and federation

ArrangementMain characteristicCommon consideration
Separate accountsEach service manages its own login.Users may need many credentials.
Single Sign-OnOne authentication experience supports multiple connected services.Failure of the shared login facility may affect access to several services.
Identity federationA relying party trusts authentication information from an identity provider.Trust, data sharing and responsibility must be governed.

SSO and federation frequently operate together, but they are not interchangeable definitions. Some SSO systems use a centrally managed account and profile. Federated arrangements specifically involve trust between an identity provider and one or more relying applications.

Convenience can create a shared point of dependence. If the common identity provider becomes unavailable or a shared account is compromised, several connected services may be affected. Strong authentication, account recovery and reliable operations remain essential.

Prelims focus

  • SSO means Single Sign-On.
  • An identity provider authenticates the user in a federated arrangement.
  • A relying party accepts permitted authentication information from the identity provider.
  • Federation can allow independently administered services to rely on a common identity provider.
  • Authentication through SSO does not remove application-specific authorization.
  • Trap: A common login does not necessarily mean that all participating services share one database or allow unrestricted data exchange.

[Sources: NIST, Digital Identity Guidelines: Federation and Assertions, SP 800-63C-4, 2025, federation model and relying parties; NIST, Digital Identity Guidelines, SP 800-63-4, 2025, glossary of Single Sign-On; Gujarat Informatics Limited, 'Gujarat Citizen Single Sign On (GOG eSuvidha),' project description; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: An identity provider authenticates the user; Service 1 controls access. Service 2 may trust the same provider without receiving all Service 1 records.
pictures.caption: Federation separates the service that authenticates a person from the service the person wishes to use.

title: Single Sign-On and Federated Digital Identity

body:
Why digital identity creates privacy questions

A digital identity system can simplify access to public services, but the information associated with it may be personal or sensitive. Name, address, date of birth, contact details, biometric characteristics and records of service use can reveal important facts about an individual.

Privacy includes an individual's interest in controlling inappropriate collection, disclosure and use of personal information. A secure authentication system should therefore do more than correctly match an identity. It should also limit who can access information, what information is collected and how long records are retained.

Key principles of responsible data handling

  • Purpose limitation: Use personal information for the legitimate purposes for which it may lawfully be processed.
  • Data minimization: Collect and use only the information reasonably necessary for the purpose.
  • Access control: Permit only authorized persons or systems to access relevant records.
  • Security: Protect information against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure and loss.
  • Accuracy: Provide appropriate means to correct inaccurate identity records.
  • Accountability: Establish clear responsibility, safeguards and appropriate complaint or redressal mechanisms.

Consent is important where the applicable law requires it, but consent alone does not make every use of personal information lawful. Applicable legal conditions and safeguards must also be satisfied.

The constitutional position: the right to privacy

In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), a 9-judge Bench of the Supreme Court unanimously recognized the right to privacy as a fundamental right protected by the Constitution. Privacy is connected with Article 21, which protects life and personal liberty, and with other rights guaranteed in Part III.

The right to privacy is not absolute. A State measure interfering with privacy must satisfy the applicable constitutional requirements, including a lawful basis and proportionality. The existence of a digital identity system does not remove these requirements.

India's digital personal data protection framework

Parliament enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which establishes a legal framework concerning digital personal data. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025. Their commencement, and the commencement of the Act's provisions, were deliberately divided into stages.

DateLegal developmentStatus at 5 November 2026
2023Digital Personal Data Protection Act enacted.Enacted; commencement is provision-specific.
13 November 2025Specified Act provisions and Rules 1, 2 and 17–21 commenced.In force.
13 November 2026Additional specified Act provisions and Rule 4 scheduled to commence.Not yet commenced at the selected cutoff.
13 May 2027Remaining major specified provisions and Rules 3, 5–16, 22 and 23 scheduled to commence.Not yet commenced at the selected cutoff.

The 2025 commencement notifications use periods of 1 year and 18 months from their publication on 13 November 2025. Therefore, it would be inaccurate to say that every substantive obligation of the Act and Rules was fully operational on 5 November 2026.

Exclusion: when an identity system prevents access

Digital exclusion occurs when a person cannot effectively use a service because of barriers such as limited connectivity, lack of a suitable device, disability, low digital literacy, incorrect records or failure of an authentication method. Exclusion can be particularly serious when access to food, healthcare, education or other essential entitlements is affected.

For example, a genuine beneficiary may have the correct identity record but be unable to complete fingerprint authentication. Another beneficiary may be unable to receive an OTP because their registered mobile number is inaccessible. These are service-access problems that should be addressed through the lawful alternative procedures available for the relevant service.

Inclusion and security are complementary goals. Removing every identity check can increase impersonation risk, while insisting on only one difficult authentication method can exclude legitimate users. A suitable system needs reliable checks and workable alternatives.

Prelims focus

  • Puttaswamy (2017): a 9-judge Supreme Court Bench recognized privacy as a fundamental right.
  • Article 21 and Part III are central to the constitutional protection of privacy.
  • The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was enacted in 2023.
  • The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified on 13 November 2025.
  • At the cutoff of 5 November 2026, commencement remained phased, with additional provisions scheduled for 13 November 2026 and 13 May 2027.
  • Trap: Enactment of a law does not necessarily mean all its provisions have commenced.

[Sources: Supreme Court of India, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, 2017, 9-judge privacy ruling; Supreme Court, Aadhaar judgment dated 26 September 2018, Part B, discussion of Puttaswamy principles; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Gazette notifications G.S.R. 843(E) and G.S.R. 846(E), both dated 13 November 2025, commencement provisions; UIDAI, Aadhaar Act, 2016, amended section 8(2); sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: India's digital personal data protection law has a phased commencement schedule.

title: Digital Identity, the Right to Privacy and the Risk of Exclusion
